- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The city installed a thirteenth hour on a Tuesday.

At first, nobody noticed. Tuesdays were already long.

The new hour appeared between 3:00 and 4:00 in the afternoon, when most people were too tired to argue with clocks. Wristwatches hesitated. Phones displayed a small gray circle. The clock above the railway station turned its hands backward, then forward, as though reconsidering an answer.

By evening, the mayor had issued a statement.

“This additional hour represents an exciting opportunity for increased productivity.”

By Wednesday, employers had claimed it.

By Thursday, parking meters had learned to charge for it.

Only the old clock repairer on Bell Street put a sign in his window:

**NO CHARGE FOR THE EXTRA HOUR.**

His name was Elias. He had been repairing clocks for forty-three years, although lately people brought him other things: a toaster, a mechanical bird, a lamp shaped like a lighthouse.

“Does it keep time?” he would ask.

“No.”

“Then I can’t promise anything.”

He usually fixed them anyway.

On the first Friday of the new hour, a girl came into his shop carrying a kitchen clock under one arm.

“It’s wrong,” she said.

Most customers said this.

“How wrong?”

“It doesn’t do the extra bit.”

She put it on the counter. It was yellow, with a painted lemon where the twelve should have been. At 3:00, its second hand continued obediently toward 4:00. Outside, every other clock in the city had entered the new hour.

Elias took off his glasses.

“Where did you get this?”

“Our kitchen.”

“Yes. Before that.”

“My mum bought it.”

“May I keep it overnight?”

The girl folded her arms.

“We need it.”

“For what?”

“To know when things happen.”

Elias considered this.

“Fair enough.”

He fetched a battered travel clock from the shelf behind him.

“A loan,” he said.

“Does that one do the extra bit?”

“Yes.”

She looked disappointed.

That night, Elias opened the yellow clock.

There was no strange mechanism inside. No hidden spring. No tiny door through which impossible afternoons might enter. Just a battery, a circuit, and a little dust.

He cleaned it. He checked the contacts. He sat with it through the extra hour the following afternoon.

The clock refused.

At 3:17, according to the yellow clock, Elias heard somebody laughing outside. Two boys were riding a shopping trolley down Bell Street. One stood inside with his arms out; the other pushed. They passed the bakery, which was closed, and the pharmacy, which was open, and disappeared around the corner.

At 3:42, a woman stopped beneath the tree opposite his shop. She put down two heavy bags and stood without doing anything at all.

Elias watched her.

He realized he had not seen anybody stand without doing anything for a very long time.

When the girl returned, he asked her name.

“June.”

“June, who lives in your house?”

“Me. My mum. Sometimes my uncle, but only when his boiler breaks.”

“And during the extra hour?”

“Mum works.”

“What do you do?”

“Wait.”

He looked at the yellow clock.

“Where?”

“School, mostly. They made another lesson. It’s called Independent Enrichment.”

“Do you like it?”

“We do worksheets.”

Elias wound the travel clock, although it did not need winding.

“Your clock is perfectly healthy,” he said.

“Then why’s it wrong?”

“I’m not sure it is.”

June took it home.

The following week, three people brought clocks that would not recognize the extra hour.

One belonged to a retired violin teacher. One had hung for twenty years in the back room of a café. The third was a watch worn by a nurse who came straight from a night shift, still carrying a packet of crackers in her coat pocket.

Elias inspected them all.

There was nothing wrong with any of them.

He began asking questions.

The violin teacher spent the extra hour playing badly, which she preferred to playing well for an audience.

The café owner closed his shutters and ate lunch with his brother.

The nurse slept.

By the end of the month, there were seventeen clocks on Elias’s shelves that kept the old time.

A reporter visited.

“Are these devices defective?”

“No.”

“Is this a protest?”

“I repair clocks.”

“Do you believe time should belong to the people?”

Elias looked annoyed.

“Whom else would it belong to?”

That sentence appeared in the newspaper above a photograph in which he looked like a man accused of stealing his own furniture.

More clocks arrived.

A bus driver brought his mother’s alarm clock. A solicitor brought a watch she had bought to celebrate making partner. June brought a friend whose clock still followed the new hour.

“What do I have to do?” the friend asked.

Elias had no answer.

“Can I stay here for a bit, then?”

He found her a stool.

She sat beside the counter and drew the clocks in a notebook. At half past three, she turned the page.

The mayor’s office sent a letter. The manufacturers sent a warning. His landlord reminded him that Bell Street was a commercial district.

Elias put all three envelopes beneath the short leg of his workbench.

By winter, there was usually someone sitting in the shop during the extra hour. June did her homework there, then complained about having done it. The nurse sometimes came to collect a repaired watch and fell asleep in the chair by the radiator.

Elias still charged for repairs. Batteries and rent had not become less expensive.

But between three and four, he made tea.

If a customer asked when their clock would be ready, he checked the workbench before answering. If someone stayed, he found another cup.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A quiet fable uses an impossible extra hour to show how institutions quickly turn new time into more work and expense.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gently wry and attentive to small acts of care. Its pathos gathers around people whose time is claimed by work, school, or obligation: June waits, the nurse sleeps, and the woman pauses beneath a tree. Elias’s modest repair shop becomes a refuge not through grand resistance but through tea, stools, and room for someone to stay. The story invites the reader to notice rest and unproductive time as needs, not defects.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds clocks, bureaucratic language, billing, and the ordinary people made to absorb an extra hour. Its moral claim is that time should belong to people, expressed through Elias’s blunt question and his small, practical hospitality. The ending favors shared rest over victory or spectacle.

## Evidence line
> He realized he had not seen anybody stand without doing anything for a very long time.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the fable is coherent and its recurring clocks, waiting, and quiet hospitality make its emphasis on protected human time distinctive within the sample.
